door.before: Today, a citizen has to find the right app among hundreds.
door.beforeSub: Different logins, different languages, different forms — and a fake portal one search result away.
door.afterSub: Every service, organised around what's happening in your life: a birth, a harvest, a first job, a pension.

rails.title: The rails are built. The door is missing.
rails.intro: India already runs the largest digital public infrastructure in the world.
rails.gap: Yet a citizen still has to know which app, which portal and which form. Saathi is the front door those rails were waiting for — built on them, not beside them.
rails.stackNote: Conceptual integrations. Saathi is not affiliated with these platforms.

why.title: These apps already exist. So why Saathi?
why.intro: India has built excellent pieces — an app full of services, a wallet of documents, a scheme finder, state portals and lakhs of help centres. Each solves one part well. But a citizen still has to know which piece to open, in which order, in which language. Saathi doesn't replace them. It is the one door that uses them for you.

tools.name: UMANG
tools.good: Thousands of central and state services in one app.
tools.missing: Organised by department — you need to know the service's name. You still fill each department's form yourself.

tools.name: DigiLocker
tools.good: Verified documents on your phone, straight from the issuer.
tools.missing: Stores documents — it doesn't apply for anything or tell you what you're owed.

tools.name: myScheme
tools.good: Finds government schemes you may be eligible for.
tools.missing: Once found, you go to each scheme's own website to apply, with a new login and form.

tools.name: State portals & e-District
tools.good: Where most services are actually delivered.
tools.missing: A different login, layout and language in every state and department.

tools.name: CSC centres
tools.good: A real person to help, in lakhs of villages and towns.
tools.missing: Means travel, a queue and a fee — for something a phone could do.

answer.title: Saathi is the front door that sits on top of all of them.
answer.body: Tell it what's happening in your life, in your language or by voice. It finds what you're owed, fills the form from DigiLocker, files it with the right department, pays by UPI — and asks before every step. The existing systems keep doing what they do best; the citizen just stops having to stitch them together.

only.title: All 22 languages and voice, on every field
only.body: Every screen, form and answer in English and all 22 scheduled languages — speak instead of typing, hear it read aloud.

only.title: Act for your parent or child

only.title: Trust you can check
only.body: No ads, no data selling. Every access to your data is logged where you can see it and switch it off, as the DPDP Act requires.

why.fair: UMANG, DigiLocker, myScheme, UPI and e-District are real, valuable government platforms; Saathi is a design concept built to work on top of them, not against them. Comparisons describe the citizen's experience today, not the engineering of these platforms.

scale.title: Built for 30 lakh requests an hour.
scale.intro: A scholarship deadline night, a PM-KISAN instalment day, an exam result at 10 AM — public services get their worst traffic all at once. Saathi is designed so that peak lands on a cache and a queue, not on a single server or a department's old database.

flow.aria: Diagram: requests from people's phones. Most are answered by a nearby copy and return at once; a small stream passes a fair gate, counters that open more windows, and a token line, on to government offices.
flow.legend: Each dot is one request. Drag the number above — a busier hour makes the dots faster, and more counters open.

people.title: Lakhs of people at once
people.body: on phones, at CSCs and helplines

nearby.title: A copy kept nearby
nearby.body: Screens and scheme pages are already on the phone and in centres across India, so most taps are answered on the spot.

gate.title: A fair entry gate
gate.body: Everyone gets a fair turn. Pressing Submit 50 times can't push anyone else out.

counters.title: Counters that open themselves
counters.body: Like a station opening more ticket windows when the crowd grows — and closing them when it's quiet.

token.title: Token line
token.body: You get your token number in a second. Your application is handled in turn — never lost, even on the busiest day.

govt.title: Government offices
govt.body: Aadhaar, DigiLocker, UPI and departments get work at a pace they can handle.

journey.title: Follow one request
journey.intro: Not every request is the same. Opening a screen, checking a status, filing an application and paying a fee each take a different path — pick one and watch where it goes, how long each stop takes, and what happens if that stop has a problem.

kinds.label: Opening a screen
kinds.summary: Sunita opens the PM-KISAN page. This is what 85 of every 100 requests look like — no server is touched at all.

steps.title: She taps PM-KISAN
steps.body: The app was installed once and keeps its screens on the phone, like a printed booklet in her pocket.

steps.title: The page opens from the nearby copy
steps.body: Scheme pages are kept on the phone and in data centres across India. The page appears at once — even on 2G.
steps.fail: No signal at all? The saved copy still opens, and anything she fills in waits on the phone until the network returns.

kinds.label: Checking status
kinds.summary: Rakesh checks where his daughter's birth certificate has reached. It needs fresh information, so it goes past the gate — but never into the main record book.

steps.title: He opens Track
steps.body: The last status he saw shows instantly from the phone, so the screen is never blank while the new one loads.

steps.title: The gate checks it's really him
steps.body: His login is checked and his turn is counted. Refreshing 100 times a minute can't slow anyone else down.
steps.fail: Too many refreshes? He's politely asked to wait a few seconds — everyone else carries on normally.

steps.title: A counter reads a quick copy of the records
steps.body: Status is read from a fast copy kept for reading, not from the main book where new applications are written. Lakhs of people can check at once without slowing down filing.
steps.fail: If the quick copy is busy, the counter reads the main book instead. Slower by a moment, never wrong.

steps.title: The new status appears
steps.body: “With Priya Nair, verification — expected in 3 days”, with a named officer and a date.

kinds.label: Submitting an application
kinds.total: 1 s to get a token number
kinds.summary: Rakesh applies for the birth certificate at 11 PM on a busy night. He gets his token number in about a second; the office does the work in turn.

steps.title: The form is saved on the phone as he types
steps.body: Every answer is kept on the phone. Hospital records come from DigiLocker, so most of the form fills itself.
steps.fail: Battery dies or the app closes? He reopens it and the form is exactly where he left it.

steps.title: He taps Submit — the gate stamps it once
steps.body: The application gets a unique stamp. Even if he taps Submit five times, it can only ever be filed once.
steps.fail: Signal drops while sending? The app sends it again by itself when the network returns — the stamp means it's never filed twice.

steps.title: A counter checks the details
steps.body: Are all the fields there? Do the documents match Aadhaar? Problems are shown to him now, in his language — not ten days later as a rejection.
steps.fail: If Aadhaar's system is slow tonight, the application is still accepted and the check finishes later. He doesn't have to wait or come back.

steps.title: It joins the token line — he gets his number
steps.body: The application is written safely in two places and gets reference BC-2026-UP-07734. From this moment it cannot be lost.
steps.fail: Even if a whole data centre goes down, the second copy carries on. Nothing he has submitted disappears.

steps.title: Nagar Nigam receives it in turn
steps.body: Applications are handed to the office at the speed its own system can take, oldest first — so a busy night never crashes the office's system.
steps.fail: If the office's system is down, the application waits in line and is retried every few minutes. Rakesh is told; nothing is lost.

steps.title: He is kept informed at every stage
steps.body: An SMS and a Track update when an officer picks it up, approves it, and when the certificate lands in his DigiLocker.

kinds.label: Paying a fee
kinds.total: about 5 s, with his own UPI app
kinds.summary: Rakesh pays ₹2,450 property tax. Money needs one extra rule: it must never be taken twice, and never lost.

steps.title: He taps Pay ₹2,450
steps.body: The amount, the office and the due date come from Nagar Nigam's own record — he doesn't type any of them.

steps.title: The gate stamps the payment once
steps.body: The payment gets a unique stamp before any money moves. However many times he taps, there can only be one payment.
steps.fail: If he taps twice by mistake, the second tap just shows the first payment — it never creates a new one.

steps.title: He approves in his own UPI app
steps.body: His bank asks for his UPI PIN — in the bank's app, not Saathi's. Saathi never sees his PIN or bank details.
steps.fail: Money taken but no confirmation? Saathi checks with the bank every few minutes until it knows: either the receipt is issued, or the money is refunded automatically within 5 days.

steps.title: The receipt is recorded
steps.body: The payment is written safely in two places and a receipt with a verification code appears at once.

steps.title: Nagar Nigam marks the tax paid
steps.body: The office's records are updated in order. If its system is busy, the receipt he already holds is his proof.

calc.label: Requests in one hour
calc.assumptions: Model: the busiest minute runs at 4× the hour's average; 85% of requests (app screens, scripts, images, scheme pages) are served by the CDN or the phone's offline cache; one service instance handles 250 requests a second at 60% load; at least 3 instances run in each of 2 regions; 12% of server requests write data; one PostgreSQL primary takes 3,000 writes a second. Design targets, to be proven with load tests — not measured on this prototype.

arch.title: For engineers: the full architecture
arch.intro: Seven layers, each one able to grow on its own. Nothing a citizen does depends on a single machine.

people.title: Citizens, CSCs and helplines
people.body: The installable app works offline and on 2G. It keeps screens and forms on the phone, so most taps never need the network at all.

edge.title: Edge: CDN, firewall, DDoS shield
edge.body: Screens, scripts and scheme pages are cached in data centres across India. Bots and floods are filtered here, before they reach anything that costs money.

gateway.title: API gateway
gateway.body: Checks the session, limits each person and each device to a fair rate, and routes the request. A citizen can't knock the system over by tapping Submit fifty times.

services.title: Stateless services that scale themselves
services.body: Small services on Kubernetes in two Indian cloud regions (MeghRaj / NIC). When load rises, more copies start in under a minute; when it falls, they stop.

queue.title: Event queue
queue.body: Submissions, payments and notifications go into a durable queue (Kafka). The citizen gets a reference number instantly; workers process in order, at the pace each department can take.

data.title: Data, split by state
data.body: PostgreSQL sharded by state, with read replicas, plus a Redis cache for hot data. Documents stay in DigiLocker — Saathi stores the reference, not a second copy.

rails.title: Government rails
rails.body: Aadhaar e-KYC, DigiLocker, UPI, PFMS and department systems are called through circuit breakers with retries and timeouts, so one slow system can't slow down the rest.

scale.movesTitle: What happens on the worst day

moves.title: Most traffic never reaches a server
moves.body: About 85% of requests are answered by the CDN or the phone's own cache. At 30 lakh requests an hour, only ~500 a second reach Saathi's servers at the peak.

moves.title: Servers multiply before the queue builds
moves.body: Autoscaling adds instances when CPU passes 60% and keeps a minimum running in both regions, even at night. Capacity follows demand instead of being guessed in advance.

moves.title: A burst becomes a line, not a crash
moves.body: If departments can't keep up, applications wait safely in the queue. Nothing is lost, the citizen already has their reference number, and Track shows where they are.

moves.title: A virtual waiting room above capacity
moves.body: If demand ever passes what's provisioned, new sessions get a fair place in line with an honest wait time — people already in the middle of a form are never cut off.

moves.title: Graceful degradation
moves.body: If Aadhaar or a department system is slow, Saathi saves the form as a draft and messages the citizen when it's through. If AI is overloaded, it falls back to the scripted, reviewed answers.

moves.title: Two regions, no single point of failure
moves.body: Each state's data is replicated to a second region. If a whole region goes down, traffic moves over in minutes, with no loss of submitted applications.

moves.title: Proven before launch
moves.body: Load tests at 2× the target peak, chaos tests that switch off servers mid-test, and live dashboards with alerts on latency and error rate — before any real citizen depends on it.

scale.honest: Honest note: the site you're using is a static prototype with no servers behind it. This page is the production design and its capacity targets — the numbers will be proven with load tests in the pilot, not claimed in advance.

split.title: One front door. A separate back room for every service.
split.intro: Citizens see one Saathi app. Behind it, every service runs on its own group of servers with its own data. When 30 lakh people are online at once, the crowd is split by what they opened — so an exam-result rush grows the Exams room alone, and a birth certificate is never slowed down by it.

split.aria: Diagram: one Saathi app sends every request to a router, which sends it to a separate lane for each service — certificates, land and farming, taxes, transport, exams and health — each with its own servers and data, and on to that department's system.

app.title: One Saathi app
app.body: the same front door for every service, in every language

router.title: Smart router
router.body: reads which service you opened and sends you to its room

dept.title: Each department's own system
dept.body: work handed over at a pace it can take

verdict.exams: Result day: the {lane} room grows to {n} servers on its own.
verdict.kisan: Payout day: the {lane} room grows to {n} servers on its own.
verdict.tax: Deadline night: the {lane} room grows to {n} servers on its own.

split.verdictTail: The other rooms don't feel it — they keep their own servers and their own data, so a birth certificate or a challan payment is as fast as on any other day. And if one room ever fails, only that service pauses; everything else keeps working.

shared.title: Shared once, used by every room
shared.intro: A few things every service needs are built once and kept very light, so they never become the bottleneck.

items.title: Login with Aadhaar OTP
items.body: You sign in once. Every room trusts the same pass, so you never log in again for each service.

items.title: Consent & privacy
items.body: One record of what you allowed, to whom and until when — every room must check it before using your data.

items.title: Notifications
items.body: One SMS and app-message service for every department, so updates reach you the same way.

items.title: Your profile & documents
items.body: Kept once, and documents stay in DigiLocker — rooms receive a reference, never a copy to store.

data.title: How the data is organised
data.intro: Splitting the servers only works if the data is split the same way. Four rules:

items.title: Each room owns its own data
items.body: The Exams room has its own database; it can't slow down or break the Certificates database, and no room reaches into another's.

items.title: Inside a room, data is split by state
items.body: Uttar Pradesh's certificates live apart from Kerala's. A rush in one state never touches another, and each state's data stays in India.

items.title: Rooms talk through one message line
items.body: When a birth certificate is issued, the Certificates room posts “certificate issued”. The Health room hears it and starts Janani Suraksha — without the two databases being tied together.

items.title: Two copies, two regions
items.body: Every room's data is written to a second region as it happens. If a data centre goes down, that room carries on from the copy, with nothing lost.

split.model: Model: 30 lakh people online at once, each making a request about every 20 seconds (1,50,000 a second); 85% answered on the phone or from the nearby copy; one server handles 250 requests a second; every room keeps at least 4 servers (2 in each region). Shares per service are illustrative. Design targets, to be proven with load tests in the pilot — not measured on this prototype.

departments.title: Both sides of the counter.
departments.intro: Every service in the app has a desk on the other side. Fifteen department consoles review applications, check e-KYC with a stated purpose, issue signed records and run challans, exams and benefit transfers — and every decision reaches the citizen in their language.
departments.frameLabel: Saathi for Departments · Nagar Nigam, Kanpur

points.title: Purpose before personal data
points.body: Aadhaar details stay masked until an officer states why — and the citizen sees that look in their privacy dashboard.

points.title: Decisions reach the citizen live
points.body: Approve, ask for a document or reject with a reason, and the citizen's app updates in the same moment.

points.title: Signed records, straight to DigiLocker
points.body: Certificates, licences and marksheets are signed digitally and land in the citizen's wallet — no printouts, no visits.

points.title: An audit trail that can't be edited
points.body: Every decision and every look at data is logged with who, when and why — for the office, the auditor and the citizen.
